name: Positional notation and place value
kb: Digits hold different values by position; ten is one and zero
note: Babylonians and Indians used this. Rome has it for decimals and whole numbers already. Not universal yet in all trades.

name: Zero as a number
kb: Zero is a digit, not absence
note: The Hindus and Arabs have this. Europe thinks zero is dangerous or meaningless. Teaching means replacing 'no tens' with 'zero tens': algebra becomes possible. Adoption slow because it threatens calculators' livelihoods.

name: Negative numbers
kb: Numbers less than zero; rules for addition and multiplication
note: Chinese and Hindu texts have them. Europe resists: 'I cannot have negative sheep.' Teaching requires understanding debt as negative property, temperature below a reference point, or mathematical convenience. Adoption requires replacing intuition with rule-following.

name: Decimal fractions
kb: Tenths, hundredths, thousandths as a continuation of positional notation past zero
note: Al-Kashi described this in the 15th century; Simon Stevin formalized it. The point or comma is merely convention. Teaching: counting by tens extends below unity. Adoption slow because it competes with fractions.

name: The decimal point convention
kb: Standardizing a marker between whole and fractional parts
note: Napier used a period; Stevin used a circle. The point won. Adoption is fast once stakes are printing. Different countries use comma still.

name: The equals sign
kb: Symbol = means both sides have the same value
note: Recorde introduced = around 1557; it replaced 'is equal to'. Before this, sentences: 'x plus 5 is the same as 12.' Afterward: x + 5 = 12. This tiny change enables algebra as a visual system.

name: Operator symbols: +, -, *, /
kb: Standardized marks for operations instead of words
note: Germany adopted + and - in 15th c. for accounting. Multiplication: earlier × (Oughtred) and · (Leibniz) both persist. Division: ÷ (Obelus) is late 17th c. Adoption is printing-driven.

name: Exponent notation
kb: Small superscript numbers for powers; x squared is x²
note: Vieta used q for quadratum (square), c for cubus. Descartes switched to superscripts. Typesetting superscripts is hard; printing adoption is slow.

name: Root symbols and radical notation
kb: Radical sign √ for square, cube, and nth roots
note: Medieval √ is a stylized r for radix. Alternative: fractional exponents (1/2 power). Teaching competing notations until one wins printing.

name: Scientific notation and powers of ten
note: Saves writing and makes comparison of magnitudes visual. Adoption requires slides rules and tables to persist; hand calculators will make it standard.

name: Metric system: standard meters, kilograms, seconds
kb: Decimal prefixes; base 10 throughout; no accidents like 12 inches to a foot
note: French Revolution, 1790s. Requires redefining all trade measures simultaneously; no gradual adoption. Professions that stake identity on old systems resist hardest: British inch, American pound. Teaching: why base 10? Because fingers. Adoption: must be enforced by law and remaking every measuring tool.

name: Dimensional analysis and unit checking
kb: Treating dimensions as algebraic quantities; force = mass times acceleration means newtons = kg⋅m/s²
note: Fourier first formalized this. Benefits: catch algebra errors (multiplying meters and kilograms is wrong), derive relationships from dimensional guess. Teaching requires algebra first.

name: Significant figures and precision rules
kb: Recording measurement uncertainty by digit count; multiplication and division rules for combining measurements
note: Requires actually knowing your apparatus uncertainty first. Teaching: students must measure things badly and see the rule explain results. Adoption in labs is slow because it exposes poor work.

name: Error propagation and uncertainty arithmetic
kb: If x has uncertainty Δx and y = f(x), then Δy = |df/dx| Δx; rules for multiple variables
note: Requires calculus and statistics both. Teaching is graduate-level. Adoption is by research groups first, later by engineering. Key insight: combine uncertainties as root-sum-square when independent, linearly when correlated.

name: Symbolic algebra and letter variables
kb: Using letters for unknown quantities; rules for manipulating equations
note: Al-Khwarizmi and medieval scholars used words; Vieta brought letters. Teaching replaces arithmetic drill with symbolic manipulation: instead of 'find the number such that when you add 5 and triple it you get 24,' write 3x + 5 = 24 and show x = 19/3. Adoption fast in universities, slow elsewhere.

name: The quadratic equation and solution formula
kb: ax² + bx + c = 0 has solution x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / 2a
note: Babylonians completed the square geometrically. Al-Khwarizmi had the method. Descartes proved it algebraically. Teaching: deriving the formula from completing the square takes an hour and feels like discovery. The ± notation is key.

name: Polynomial equations and factoring
kb: Expressions like x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3); finding roots
note: Cubics and quartics have closed formulas (Cardano, Ferrari), but they are ugly. Quintics do not have formulas (Galois, Abel). Teaching: show a cubic solved by substitution and depression. Adoption: essential for engineering, slow elsewhere.

name: Binomial theorem and binomial expansion
kb: (x + y)ⁿ expands to a sum of terms with binomial coefficients C(n,k)
note: Newton discovered this; Pascal's triangle gives coefficients. Teaching: why does (x+y)² = x² + 2xy + y²? Draw a square divided into four. Why does (x+y)³ work the same way? Induction proof follows. Adoption: fast, because it saves multiplication.

name: Logarithm as inverse exponent: log₁₀(1000) = 3
kb: If b^x = a, then log_b(a) = x; rules: log(xy) = log(x) + log(y)
note: Napier invented this to replace multiplication with addition: multiply by looking up logs, adding, looking up antilog. Teaching: understand exponent rules first. Then log is just naming the exponent. The product rule is obvious once you see it.

name: Infinite series and convergence
kb: Sum of infinitely many terms: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... = 2; when does it converge?
note: Zeno's paradox and medieval scholars debated infinities. Newton and Leibniz used series for trig and exp. Teaching requires the limit concept first. Convergence tests (ratio, integral, comparison) come later.

name: The limit and convergence to a value
kb: As x → a, f(x) → L means values cluster arbitrarily close to L; formal: for any ε > 0, choose δ > 0 such that |x - a| < δ implies |f(x) - L| < ε
note: The foundation of modern calculus, formalized by Cauchy and Weierstrass. Medieval debates about infinitesimals; Newton and Leibniz avoided the rigour. Teaching: intuitive first ('get as close as you want'), then epsilon-delta proof for one simple case. Adoption is graduate-level.

name: The derivative as instantaneous rate of change
kb: f'(x) = lim[h→0] (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h; rules: product, chain, quotient
note: Newton's fluxions, Leibniz's differential notation (df/dx) is cleaner. Teaching: slope of a curve at a point, velocity as change of position, acceleration as change of velocity. First application to physics and engineering. Adoption: essential for all quantitative science.

name: The integral as area under a curve
kb: ∫f(x)dx is the area under f; fundamental theorem: antiderivative of f has derivative f
note: Riemann formalized it; Lebesgue generalized later. Teaching: Archimedes estimated area with inscribed and circumscribed rectangles. Calculus makes it algebraic. Adoption: once differentiation exists, integrals follow for work, volume, mass.

name: Fundamental theorem: differentiation and integration are inverses
kb: d/dx ∫f = f and ∫df/dx = f; connects rate of change to total change
note: Proven by Newton and Leibniz independently. Teaching is the eureka moment: derivative and integral undo each other. Adoption is fast because it makes calculations feasible.

name: Ordinary differential equations and solution methods
kb: Equations like y' = -ky describe decay or growth; separation of variables, integrating factors
note: Newton's laws are ODEs. Teaching: simple cases first (y' = 2y has solution e^(2x)). Adoption: essential for physics and engineering.

name: Partial differential equations
kb: Equations with derivatives with respect to multiple variables; heat, wave, Laplace equations
note: d²u/dt² = c² d²u/dx² (wave equation); solutions require boundary conditions. Teaching is hard; Fourier series helps. Adoption is by mathematical physicists first.

name: Fourier series: decomposing periodic functions
kb: Any periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines with the right amplitudes and phases
note: Fourier solved heat equation using this. Teaching: mechanical analogy using tuning forks and resonance. Adoption: electrical engineering relies on it for AC power.

name: Fourier transform and continuous frequency spectrum
kb: Generalizing Fourier series to non-periodic signals; converting between time and frequency domains
note: Integral form goes to infinity. Teaching requires confidence with Fourier series first. Adoption is late 20th century for digital signal processing.

name: Complex numbers: a + bi where i² = -1
kb: Quadratics always have solutions in complex numbers; polar form re^(iθ); Euler's e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ
note: Cardano's cubic formula forced complex intermediate steps. Teaching: geometry (rotation and scaling in the plane) makes it tangible. Adoption: fast in AC electricity and physics.

name: Vectors and vector algebra
kb: Directed quantities; dot product a·b = |a||b|cos(angle); cross product a×b perpendicular to both
note: Gibbs and Heaviside developed notation independently in the 1880s. Teaching: forces, velocities, displacements. Adoption: essential for 3D mechanics.

name: Matrices and matrix multiplication
kb: Rectangular arrays of numbers; AB is not the same as BA; determinant measures invertibility
note: Cayley formalized (1858). Teaching: transforms (rotation, scaling); systems of equations as Ax = b. Adoption: slow until computers make it practical.

name: Determinants and matrix inversion
kb: det(A) = 0 means A is singular (non-invertible); A⁻¹ exists if det(A) ≠ 0
note: Ancient roots in solving simultaneous equations. Teaching: area and volume interpretation. Adoption by applied mathematicians first.

name: Tensors and tensor notation
kb: Generalizing scalars, vectors, matrices; stress is a tensor (force per unit area in each direction)
note: Einstein summation convention hides indices. Teaching requires patience. Adoption: essential for solid mechanics and general relativity.

name: Numerical methods: Newton-Raphson, bisection, iteration
kb: Algorithms to find roots or solve equations when closed forms do not exist; choosing method depends on smoothness and number of solutions
note: Requires testing convergence by hand before computers. Teaching: graph on paper, subdivide, iterate. Adoption: essential for any real design calculation.

name: Polynomial interpolation and finite differences
kb: Given n points, unique polynomial of degree n-1 passes through them; Newton forward differences for tables
note: Computing machines depend on difference tables. Teaching: Lagrange vs. Newton forms. Adoption: essential for any function tabulation.

name: Least squares method and curve fitting
kb: Minimize sum of squared errors between data points and model; normal equations from setting derivatives to zero
note: Gauss and Legendre derived independently (1805-1812). Teaching: why squares? They weight large errors heavily and math is neat. Adoption: fast in geodesy and later in all experimental science.

name: Coordinate geometry and the Cartesian plane
kb: Representing curves as equations: circle is x² + y² = r²; line is ax + by + c = 0
note: Descartes and Fermat, early 1600s. Teaching: each point is a pair (x,y); equations become curves. Adoption: fast in university, slow in practical surveying.

name: Conic sections: circles, ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas
kb: All are second-degree equations ax² + bxy + cy² + dx + ey + f = 0; eccentricity e determines shape
note: Apollonius knew them geometrically. Descartes wrote them algebraically. Teaching: derive from plane cutting a cone, or as locus of points. Adoption: essential for understanding planetary orbits.

name: Trigonometric functions and tables
kb: sin, cos, tan; inverse functions; tables for every degree or tenth of degree; identities like sin² + cos² = 1
note: Hipparchus computed chord tables; Indians used sines. Modern tables (7-decimal, 15-decimal) require thousands of hours to compute and check. Manufacturing tables is expensive; printing enables adoption.

name: Spherical trigonometry and navigation formulas
kb: Solving triangles on a sphere; great circles; spherical excess; rhumb line vs. geodesic
note: Essential for celestial navigation and map-making. Teaching requires globe and accurate diagrams. Adoption: fast among navigators and cartographers.

name: Descriptive geometry and engineering drawing
kb: Three orthographic views (top, front, side) fully describe a 3D object; sections; auxiliary views
note: Monge formalized it for military engineering (1780s). Teaching: start with wooden blocks, draw them, build from the drawing. Adoption: universal by 1850 in all engineering.

name: Non-Euclidean geometry: hyperbolic and elliptic
kb: Gauss, Lobachevsky, Riemann: parallel postulate is independent; curved spaces have their own geometry
note: Shocking because Euclidean seemed necessary. Teaching requires intrinsic vs. extrinsic curvature. Adoption: slow until Einstein (1915) makes gravity a curved spacetime.

name: Differential geometry: curves and surfaces
kb: Curvature, torsion, geodesics, Gaussian curvature, first and second fundamental forms
note: Gauss and Riemann. Teaching requires calculus and linear algebra. Adoption by theoretical physics and later differential geometry becomes essential.

name: Permutations and combinations
kb: nPr = n!/(n-r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!); binomial coefficients C(n,k)
note: Ancient roots; Pascal systematized. Teaching: counting in two ways (order matters or not). Adoption: fast in gambling and later in all statistics.

name: Probability axioms and conditional probability
kb: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B); Bayes' theorem
note: Formalized by Kolmogorov (1933). Teaching starts with dice and urn problems. Adoption: essential for statistics once this century opens.

name: Normal (Gaussian) distribution and the bell curve
kb: f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)); most natural distribution for sums of independent errors
note: Gauss, Laplace, de Moivre. Teaching: derive from sums of dice or measurements. Adoption: universal in any quantitative field.

name: Central limit theorem
kb: Sum of many independent random variables is approximately normal, regardless of their individual distributions
note: Explains why normal distribution is universal. Teaching requires multiple simulations to convince. Adoption: theoretical foundation for all inferential statistics.

name: Mean, variance, and standard deviation
kb: Mean μ = sum/n; variance σ² = average squared deviation; standard deviation σ = √(variance)
note: Quetelet popularized mean and variance (1830s). Teaching: compute by hand for small datasets. Adoption: fast in any measurement discipline.

name: Correlation and covariance
kb: Pearson r = Σ(x-μx)(y-μy) / (n σx σy); r ranges from -1 to +1; r² is fraction of variance explained
note: Galton and Pearson (1880s). Teaching: scatter plot with best-fit line. Adoption: essential for social science and medicine.

name: Linear regression and the line of best fit
kb: y = a + bx where b = r(σy/σx); minimizes squared vertical distances
note: Legendre and Gauss (1805-1812); refined by Pearson. Teaching: fit to data, predict new y from new x. Adoption: universal in experiments.

name: Student's t-test for mean differences
kb: t = (mean1 - mean2) / (SE of difference); compares two small samples
note: Gosset (pseudonym 'Student', 1908) working in brewing. Teaching requires Student's t distribution tables. Adoption: universal in comparing experiments.

name: Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
kb: Partitions variance into groups and residuals; F-test whether group means differ
note: Fisher (1920s). Teaching: one-way then multi-way. Adoption by agricultural and later all experimental science.

name: Sampling theory and the standard error
kb: SE = σ/√n; determines precision of sample mean estimate; confidence interval is mean ± t*SE
note: Practical foundation for all surveys. Teaching: simulate draws from a population. Adoption: fast in quality control.

name: Confidence interval and margin of error
kb: 95% CI is estimate ± 1.96 SE; if we repeat the survey 100 times, about 95 contain the true value
note: Common misunderstanding: the interval is random, not the parameter. Teaching requires clarification. Adoption: standard in polls and clinical trials.

name: Significance test and p-value
kb: p is probability of data if null hypothesis is true; p < 0.05 usually means reject null
note: Fisher popularized p-value; Neyman-Pearson developed hypothesis testing framework. Teaching: both ideas matter but are often confused. Adoption: dominant but controversial by end of 20th century.

name: Randomisation and random assignment
kb: Assigning subjects to treatment or control by random mechanism ensures balance on unknown confounders
note: Fisher advocated it for agricultural trials. Teaching: why matters (controls bias), how to do it (draw lots, random number table). Adoption is slow because it requires surrendering control.

name: Blocking and stratification in experiments
kb: Divide subjects into homogeneous blocks, randomise within block, to reduce variance from known confounders
note: Fisher (1925). Teaching: you know some subjects are different (male/female, old/young); use this. Adoption: standard in agricultural and medical experiments.

name: Control group and negative control
kb: Run the same experiment without treatment to measure placebo effect and natural variation
note: Medical tradition going back centuries (though not formalized). Teaching: without it, cannot distinguish treatment from natural history. Adoption is slow in medicine because 'denying' treatment feels unethical.

name: Blinding and double-blind experiments
kb: Neither subject nor experimenter knows who got treatment; reveals biases in observation and reporting
note: Placebo effect is real and unconscious bias is universal. Teaching: show a color-changing experiment (nothing actually changed) then 'explain' it to subjects, whose reports change. Adoption is slow because it requires admitting fallibility.

name: Mortality table and actuarial science
kb: Probability of death at each age; lx survivors at age x; ex life expectancy
note: Graunt (1662) from London bills of mortality. Teaching: data is public; computation is rote. Adoption: fast in insurance once mathematics spreads.

name: Control chart and statistical process control
kb: Plot process output over time with control limits (μ ± 3σ); trends or excursions signal problems
note: Shewhart (1920s) at Western Electric. Teaching: time series is as important as variation. Adoption: transforms quality control from inspection to prediction.

name: Statics and forces in equilibrium
kb: Leverage, moments, center of gravity; force balance and moment balance
note: Archimedes knew this. Rome has it thoroughly. Teaching is engineering curriculum baseline.

name: Kinematics: position, velocity, acceleration
kb: v = dx/dt; a = dv/dt; for constant acceleration, x = x0 + v0*t + (1/2)*a*t²
note: Ancient scholars attempted this without calculus. Teaching is trivial after derivatives exist. Adoption: immediate in physics and engineering.

name: Newton's three laws of motion
kb: 1) No force, no change. 2) F = ma. 3) Action equals reaction
note: Principia (1687). Teaching: Galileo and Descartes prepared the ground. Adoption: transforms all engineering from qualitative to quantitative.

name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
kb: F = G m1 m2 / r²; same law governs apples and planets
note: Explains Kepler's laws. Teaching: derives planetary orbits. Adoption: transforms astronomy and physics into unified science.

name: Momentum and impulse
kb: p = mv; dp/dt = F; momentum is conserved when external forces are zero
note: Descartes understood conservation; Newton formalized. Teaching: collisions and explosions. Adoption: immediate.

name: Kinetic energy and potential energy
kb: KE = (1/2) m v²; PE = mgh; energy is conserved when forces are conservative
note: Leibniz introduced vis viva (living force). Teaching: energy is useful even when forces are complex. Adoption: fast in engineering.

name: Work, power, and efficiency
kb: Work W = F · d (force dot displacement); power P = dW/dt; efficiency = output/input
note: Defining work and power makes engine efficiency measurable. Teaching: mechanical advantage vs. power (pulleys help force, not power). Adoption: immediate and universal.

name: Elasticity and Hooke's law
kb: Stress σ = F/A (force per area); strain ε = ΔL/L (fractional change); E = σ/ε (Young's modulus)
note: Hooke (1678) discovered spring law; generalized to materials by Thomas Young (1807). Teaching: why materials behave differently. Adoption: foundation for structural engineering.

name: Fluid statics and buoyancy
kb: Pressure P = ρ g h (density times gravity times depth); Archimedes' principle
note: Archimedes and Hero knew it. Teaching: submerged objects. Adoption: immediate in navigation and dam engineering.

name: Hydrodynamics and Bernoulli's equation
kb: P + (1/2) ρ v² + ρ g h = constant along streamline; relates pressure, velocity, height
note: Bernoulli (1738). Teaching: high velocity means low pressure (why wind lifts roofs). Adoption: essential for pumps, pipes, and aerodynamics.

name: Viscosity and Newton's law of friction
kb: Shear stress τ = η (dv/dy); viscosity η depends on fluid and temperature; Stokes drag
note: Newton described it qualitatively; Stokes derived drag force on spheres (1851). Teaching: oiliness is measurable. Adoption: essential for lubrication and later fluid mechanics.

name: Reynolds number and flow regime
kb: Re = (ρ v L) / η; low Re is viscous (creeping) flow, high Re is turbulent
note: Reynolds (1883). Teaching: same flow pattern works at all scales if Re is same. Adoption: essential for aerodynamics and pipeline design.

name: Aerodynamic lift and wing design
kb: Pressure difference between upper and lower surfaces due to velocity difference; L = (1/2) ρ v² A CL
note: Kutta-Joukowski theorem (1902-1906). Teaching requires wind tunnel or theoretical derivation. Adoption: transforms aviation from dream to engineering.

name: Acoustics and sound propagation
kb: Sound speed v = √(K/ρ) where K is bulk modulus; intensity I = (1/2) ρ v (p0)²
note: Newton and Laplace debated whether sound is isothermal or adiabatic. Teaching: waves, not particles. Adoption: slow until mechanical reproduction creates demand.

name: Wave motion and the wave equation
kb: ∂²u/∂t² = v² ∂²u/∂x²; solutions are traveling and standing waves
note: d'Alembert (1746). Teaching: mechanical analogy (vibrating string) then abstract. Adoption: essential for understanding vibration, sound, and later light and matter waves.

name: Geometric optics and ray tracing
kb: Light travels in straight rays; reflects at angle of incidence; refracts by Snell's law n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2
note: Fermat's principle (light takes fastest path) explains both laws. Teaching: mirrors and lenses. Adoption: immediate in designing instruments.

name: Diffraction and Fraunhofer patterns
kb: Light bends around edges and slits; diffraction grating has many slits for high resolution
note: Fraunhofer (1819-1823). Teaching: how gratings work (parallel slits). Adoption: transforms spectroscopy.

name: Electromagnetic spectrum
kb: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays; all c/λ = f
note: Visible is tiny fraction (400-700 nm). Teaching: infrared feels like heat, UV causes sunburn, X-rays penetrate flesh. Adoption: telescopes and later radio.

name: Electrostatics and Coulomb's law
kb: F = k q1 q2 / r²; like gravity but for electric charge; field E = F/q
note: Coulomb (1785). Teaching: electric field is the concept; force follows. Adoption: foundation for all electric phenomena.

name: Magnetostatics and magnetic field
kb: Magnetic field B; dipole moment m; torque τ = m × B; force on current F = I L × B
note: Ampere and Gauss. Teaching: bar magnet, compass, current loop. Adoption: immediate in motors and generators.

name: Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic theory
kb: Four equations unify electricity, magnetism, and light; predict electromagnetic waves
note: Maxwell (1861-1862). Teaching: each equation is comprehensible; together they are profound. Adoption is slow because it requires accepting light is electromagnetic.

name: Electromagnetic wave and radiation
kb: Oscillating E and B fields perpendicular to each other and direction of travel; speed c = 1/√(ε0 μ0)
note: Light IS an electromagnetic wave. Teaching: Hertz demonstrated (1887-1888). Adoption: transforms radio and later all wireless communication.

name: Speed of light as fundamental constant
kb: c ≈ 3 × 10^8 m/s; same in all inertial reference frames; appears in E = mc²
note: Galileo, Roemer, Foucault, Bradley all attempted measurement. Teaching: why is it special? Adoption: slow until Einstein.

name: Kinetic theory of gases
kb: Gas pressure is momentum transfer from colliding molecules; P = (1/3) ρ <v²>; explains ideal gas law
note: Clausius, Maxwell, Boltzmann (1860s-1870s). Teaching: one molecule has no pressure; billions do. Adoption: transforms thermodynamics from empirical to theoretical.

name: Statistical mechanics and ensemble theory
kb: Macroscopic properties from microstate probabilities; Boltzmann distribution P(E) ~ exp(-E/kT)
note: Boltzmann, Gibbs (1870s-1890s). Teaching requires probability and quantum mechanics for full understanding. Adoption by theoretical physicists first.

name: Boltzmann distribution and thermal equilibrium
kb: Probability of state with energy E is proportional to exp(-E/kT); explains chemical equilibrium
note: Everything is exponential: molecular speeds, electron energy levels, reaction rates. Teaching: why ln(k) vs 1/T is linear (Arrhenius equation). Adoption: universal in chemistry and physics.

name: Blackbody radiation and Planck's law
kb: Energy density u(ν,T) = (8πhν³/c³) / (exp(hν/kT) - 1); Rayleigh-Jeans fails at high ν
note: Ultraviolet catastrophe and Planck's quantum fix (1900). Teaching: experiment shows curve; classical theory predicts infinite intensity at high frequency. Teaching point: sometimes you must invent new physics.

name: The quantum and photon concept
kb: Light is quantised in packets of energy E = hν; Planck constant h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J⋅s
note: Planck (1900) solved blackbody; Einstein (1905) applied to photoelectric effect. Teaching: why is h so small? Why can't we see energy packets in everyday light (because intensity is huge). Adoption: slow, even Einstein was reluctant.

name: Photoelectric effect and stopping potential
kb: Light knocks electrons from metal; E = hν - φ (work function); proves photon hypothesis
note: Millikan measured stopping potential (1916). Teaching: light intensity does not matter, only frequency. This seemed absurd to everyone. Adoption took Einstein's Nobel Prize (1921) as proof.

name: Wave mechanics and Schrödinger equation
kb: Ψ(x,t) is wave function; |Ψ|² is probability density; iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t = -ℏ²/2m ∇²Ψ + V Ψ
note: Schrödinger (1926). Teaching is technically hard and philosophically confusing (wave vs particle). Adoption: slow but now universal in quantum chemistry.

name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
kb: Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2; cannot know position and momentum simultaneously with arbitrary precision
note: Heisenberg (1927). Teaching: not instrument limitation, but fundamental. Adoption: slow because it contradicts intuition.

name: The nucleus and radioactivity
kb: Rutherford showed atoms have tiny dense nuclei; three types of radiation (alpha, beta, gamma)
note: Rutherford (1911); radioactivity discovered by Becquerel, explained by Rutherford and Soddy. Teaching: gold foil experiment shows nuclear structure. Adoption: opens nuclear physics.

name: The neutron
kb: Neutral nuclear particle; mass nearly equals proton; Chadwick proved (1932) from alpha bombardment
note: Completes the picture: nucleus is protons and neutrons. Teaching: beta decay produces electron and antineutrino (not just released from nucleus). Adoption: opens path to fission.

name: Nuclear fission and chain reaction
kb: Heavy nucleus splits into fragments; releases neutrons and 200 MeV; self-sustaining chain if k > 1
note: Meitner and Frisch (1938-1939); Manhattan Project (1942-1945). Teaching: Einstein's E = mc², mass defect, reaction rates. Adoption: immediate military application (bomb and reactor).

name: Controlled experiment and causality
kb: Manipulate one variable (treatment), hold others constant, measure outcome; compare to control
note: Foundation of empirical science. Teaching: why matters (isolates cause from correlation). Adoption is slow because it requires surrendering real-world complexity.

name: Hypothesis and prediction
kb: Propose specific prediction from theory; design experiment to test it; null hypothesis is baseline
note: Explicit prediction, not 'let's see what happens.' Teaching: why falsifiable matters. Adoption: becomes standard in quantitative science.

name: Replication and repeatability
kb: Another researcher, different time and place, obtains same results with same methods
note: Validates findings and catches fraud. Teaching: why peer skepticism matters. Adoption: slow because replication is unglamorous and often unrewarding.

name: Laboratory notebook and data recording
kb: Daily record of observations, conditions, calculations, false starts; dated, sequential, no erasure
note: Legal requirement for patent disputes. Teaching: why matters (reproducibility, chain of custody). Adoption: fast in experimental labs.

name: Negative result and null finding
kb: Experiment where predicted effect did not occur; equally valid as positive, often more informative
note: Publication bias: journals reject negatives. Teaching: why matters (saves others' time). Adoption: slow because negatives disappoint.

name: Peer criticism and expert review
kb: Colleagues check logic, methods, calculations; public critique in meetings or correspondence
note: Royal Society tradition. Teaching: why defensiveness fails. Adoption: fast in university but slow in industry and government.

name: Learned society and academy
kb: Membership of scientists; regular meetings; publications; elect fellows; set standards
note: Royal Society (1660), Academie des Sciences (1666). Teaching: creates community and authority. Adoption: fast among elite, slow elsewhere.

name: Scientific journal and periodical
kb: Monthly or quarterly publication of peer-reviewed articles with title, methods, results, discussion
note: Philosophical Transactions (1665) first. Teaching: establishes priority and enables distant researchers. Adoption: fast once printing enables it.

name: Referee and peer review
kb: Editor sends manuscript to expert referees anonymously; accepts or rejects based on review
note: Formalised in 20th century (Nature and Science). Teaching: why anonymous matters (prevents conflicts). Adoption: slow because refereeing is unpaid.

name: Citation and bibliographic reference
kb: Footnote naming source of idea or fact; enables tracking influence and crediting prior work
note: Standard notation evolved over centuries (now many styles). Teaching: plagiarism vs. citation. Adoption: fast once journals exist.

name: Textbook and codified knowledge
kb: Book that teaches subject from first principles; worked examples; exercises with answers
note: Euclid's Elements (300 BC) set standard. Teaching: distill knowledge into digestible form. Adoption: slow because good textbooks take years to write and refine.

name: Curriculum and course sequence
kb: Planned sequence of courses building toward degree; prerequisites ensure logical progression
note: Universities formalized in medieval period. Teaching: what order? Arithmetic before algebra, geometry before calculus. Adoption: slow because schools resist change.

name: Examination and credentialing
kb: Written or oral test to verify mastery; degree or certificate signals to employers
note: Universities began written exams in 19th century. Teaching: standardises quality. Adoption: slow because it threatens existing credentials.

name: Doctorate and research degree
kb: PhD requires original research contribution; defended before experts; credential for independent researcher
note: German universities formalised (1800s). Teaching: what counts as original? How evaluate quality? Adoption: now universal marker of research qualification.

name: Research group and principal investigator
kb: Senior scientist leads team of postdocs and students; collective work; shared credit
note: Liebig's group (1830s) was model. Teaching: how supervise and credit work. Adoption: fast in universities, slow in industry.

name: Funded research programme
kb: Government or foundation grants money for specific research goals; researcher proposes, peer review decides
note: NIH, NSF, DFIR modern examples. Teaching: how write proposal. Adoption: became essential by 1950s as research became expensive.

name: Patent as disclosure and property right
kb: Technical description filed with government; grants monopoly for term; requires disclosure of how it works
note: English statute 1624. Teaching: why disclose? Fear of copying drives secrecy. Patent law forces choice: publish or abandon claim. Adoption is slow and contested.
